title: AI procurement: Deployed outcomes outrank adoption counts
desc: Advocates lifecycle evaluation, tailored contracts, data rights and exit capacity instead of vendor demonstrations or purchase price alone.

kps.k: This cluster treats AI governance as a procurement and institutional-learning problem: buyers need evidence of deployed value, not adoption counts or vendor demonstrations.
kps.d: M-25-22 supplies an operational federal procurement framework; GAO examines acquisition practice; The Law of Evaluation argues for connecting AI oversight to administrative law and causal evaluation. Their convergence does not establish that AI improves services or that the proposed safeguards work universally. GAO reviewed a nongeneralizable sample of 13 acquisitions covering 44 contracts and agreements at four agencies, alongside Commerce initiatives. The article's adoption surveys provide context rather than causal evidence, and the memorandum presents efficiency as an opportunity rather than a measured result.

qs.q: By situating AI evaluation within the wider landscape of federal performance measurement, evidence-based policymaking, and procurement quality assurance, we argue that effective AI governance requires reconnecting the emerging AI toolkit with longstanding evaluation obligations in administrative and procurement law.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

qs.q: To assess the extent to which selected agencies are prepared to share knowledge about AI acquisitions as directed by the recent OMB guidance, we assessed requirements in M-25-22 and interviewed senior acquisition leaders and officials from our nongeneralizable sample about how, if at all, they documented lessons learned.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Evaluation should measure real-world outcomes against existing practice and continue throughout deployment.
kps.d: M-25-22 requires practicable proposal testing and contractual rights to regular evaluation, with metrics tied to mission outcomes and baseline performance. The Law of Evaluation goes further: benchmarks, red-teaming and audits do not by themselves establish causal effects, so consequential deployments warrant rigorous pilots or randomised trials against actual, potentially flawed human practices. It proposes annual performance measurement, ongoing quality assurance and more intensive impact evaluation for high-stakes projects. GAO reports that agencies struggle to select suitable tests; NIST officials caution that universal tests do not yet exist. The article acknowledges trial costs and argues that agentic systems require workflow-level assessment of accuracy, safety, escalation and recovery over time.

qs.q: When determining whether to include                   performance-based incentives, agencies must carefully consider whether the                   established metrics are correctly tied to desired business and mission outcomes,                   and whether they can adequately measure baseline performance of the AI systems                   or services.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Second, they address the thorny challenge of imperfect human baselines – where human performance might itself be biased or error-prone – by avoiding the trap of holding AI to unrealistic standards (such as zero bias) when the relevant comparison should be to existing practices.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Procurement speed creates a trade-off with tailored safeguards, rather than a clear choice between good and bad acquisition methods.
kps.d: GAO reports that deliberate agency-led procurement can secure suitable terms but slow adoption, while vendor upgrades and existing contracts can accelerate delivery without adequate AI-specific protections. FEMA officials said an expedient existing contract prevented them from requiring post-award testing. GAO also identifies accountability and transparency risks in flexible non-FAR agreements. M-25-22 seeks flexibility through outcome-based specifications without abandoning monitoring. GAO's examples of small initial testing contracts and Agile delivery suggest ways to combine experimentation with staged commitment, but remain illustrative; GAO does not identify a universally superior approach.

qs.q: They determined that using an existing contract was more expedient but limited the specific AI terms and conditions they could include.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: SOO                   and PWS provide agencies with more flexibility to acquire AI systems or services                   that meet agencies' outcome-based needs, but may not meet unnecessary or                   overly-limiting requirements in Statements of Work (SOW).
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Contracts determine whether buyers can test systems, protect data and hold vendors accountable.
kps.d: GAO documents practical failures: FEMA lacked rights to share model outputs, and Maven strengthened follow-on contracts after early requirements proved inadequate for vendor accountability. M-25-22 requires clear ownership and IP terms, privacy protections, vendor cooperation with independent evaluation and internal disclosure of testing procedures and results. It permits closely monitored vendor testing when appropriate rather than requiring every test to be external. The Law of Evaluation proposes stronger protection: expressly making no-testing and no-benchmarking clauses unenforceable for rights- and safety-impacting AI and clarifying safeguarded access for independent evaluators. Those proposals extend or clarify existing obligations; they are not findings that every restrictive clause is already expressly invalid.

qs.q: Maven officials reported learning that their early contracts lacked AI-related requirements needed to hold vendors accountable, and they added increasingly defined AI-related requirements in follow-on contracts.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Value for money depends on lifecycle costs, continued performance and the ability to exit—not simply the initial purchase price.
kps.d: GAO reports uncertainty about licensing and overlooked infrastructure costs. Army officials rejected a proposal that would have exceeded $500 million annually in licensing; this was projected cost, not expenditure. VA retired SoKAT after judging its improvements insufficient to justify added cost. GAO's qualified preference for service acquisition reflects ongoing assessment needs, not a universal purchasing rule. M-25-22 recommends pricing transparency, portability, interoperability, periodic comparative value reviews, rollback provisions and sunset criteria. Together, these measures aim to preserve competition and make renewal contingent on continuing value rather than vendor dependency.

qs.q: That proposal would have resulted in more than $500 million each year just for licensing fees in addition to the cost to acquire the vehicles.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Protections against vendor lock-in can    vary, but include requirements for vendor knowledge transfers, data and model    portability, providing agencies with rights to code and models produced in    performance of a contract, and transparency in licensing and pricing.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The central institutional disagreement concerns whether existing legal processes can deliver meaningful oversight or merely formal compliance.
kps.d: The sources largely agree on the need for evaluation; they differ in emphasis rather than presenting opposing empirical findings. The Law of Evaluation argues that existing performance, evidence-building and procurement law provide a foundation, while acknowledging objections about performative metrics. It reports that DHS's 2025 evaluation plan omitted AI despite 26 reported rights-impacting applications in 2024, and that ATS performance targets omitted accuracy, false positives and timeliness. Its answer combines outcome-specific metrics, independent access, adequate funding and consequences for failure. GAO's reported expertise shortages reinforce the capacity constraint. Executive guidance also remains politically revisable, and M-25-22 has phased applicability and exclusions for Intelligence Community elements and National Security System components.

qs.q: Yet nowhere in these performance measures is any metric of the accuracy of the system or false positives, nor is there any measure relating to timeliness.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

qs.q: **Access to subject matter experts.** Officials from each of our five selected agencies told us that limited access to subject matter experts, such as data scientists and software engineers, was a challenge for procuring AI technologies.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Institutional learning must capture failures and feed later purchasing decisions; repositories alone cannot supply that knowledge.
kps.d: M-25-22 directs development of shared procurement resources and encourages agency contributions. GAO finds that DOD, DHS, GSA and VA lacked formal requirements or processes for systematically documenting lessons as of September 2025. Undocumented SoKAT lessons and FEMA classification limitations illustrate knowledge that later buyers could lose. GAO recommends mandatory collection at all four agencies; their concurrence does not establish completed implementation. The Law of Evaluation extends the practical lesson to private buyers, recommending workflow experiments, external evaluation rights and access to test suites, error analyses and quality-assurance plans. Its suggestion that credible validation can differentiate vendors remains a prospective market claim.

qs.q: Our review of the four agencies’ departmental AI policies confirmed that none of the policies include a formal requirement or process to consistently document lessons learned even though some articulate their value.[fn50] Senior leaders confirmed that the departmental policies in effect as of September 2025 do not require agency officials to systematically document lessons learned from AI acquisitions.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Buyers should refuse “no testing” provisions, insist on clauses that expressly permit experimentation and external evaluation, and treat access to evaluation artifacts—test suites, error analyses, quality-assurance plans—as part of the product rather than a discretionary add-on.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The academia-and-research source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that AI procurement should be governed by evidence of deployed outcomes rather than adoption counts, internal benchmarks or vendor demonstrations. It materially extends that proposition by embedding lifecycle evaluation in administrative and procurement law: causal comparison with existing practice, risk-tiered testing, ongoing quality assurance, independent review, buyer access to evaluation artifacts and enforceable contractual testing rights. Its central reason is epistemic and institutional: pre-deployment benchmarks and demonstrations cannot establish real-world effects, while existing legal processes provide potential mechanisms for measurement and accountability. The source nevertheless identifies important internal qualifications. Rigorous methods such as randomised trials are resource-intensive; agentic systems require workflow-level monitoring over time; executive guidance is politically reversible; and nominal evaluation duties can become compliance theatre when metrics omit accuracy, error costs or timeliness. These cautions do not weaken its overall support. Instead, they motivate its concrete additions—risk-based evaluation intensity, funded independent expertise, data infrastructure, periodic revalidation and consequences for vendors or systems that fail evaluation. This assessment concerns the supplied academic source and should not be read as representative of academia generally.

qs.q: Third, causal methods address the fundamental epistemic uncertainty about how AI systems will affect outcomes in the real world, moving beyond predictions about what might happen to evidence about what does happen once these systems are deployed.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Buyers should refuse “no testing” provisions, insist on clauses that expressly permit experimentation and external evaluation, and treat access to evaluation artifacts—test suites, error analyses, quality-assurance plans—as part of the product rather than a discretionary add-on.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The supplied regulator and oversight sources accept the proposition that AI procurement should be judged by deployed outcomes and governed across the lifecycle, then materially develop it into concrete institutional practice. M-25-22 provides the prescriptive architecture: outcome-linked metrics and baselines, realistic pre-award testing, continuing contractual evaluation, data and IP protections, portability, lifecycle-cost reviews and exit criteria. GAO complements that framework with evidence from selected federal acquisitions and a specific institutional-learning reform: agencies should systematically capture and reuse lessons, including from unsuccessful or limited-performing deployments. Material variation lies in role and evidentiary posture. M-25-22 presents governance requirements and recommendations while treating efficiency as an opportunity, not a demonstrated result; GAO documents practical failures and trade-offs but expressly limits generalisation from its sample and concludes that no procurement approach is yet universally superior. Thus, these curated sources strengthen and operationalise the proposition without establishing that the safeguards always work or that AI itself improves services.

qs.q: When determining whether to include                   performance-based incentives, agencies must carefully consider whether the                   established metrics are correctly tied to desired business and mission outcomes,                   and whether they can adequately measure baseline performance of the AI systems                   or services.
qs.a: M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Specifically, GAO is recommending that DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA update their policies to require officials to systematically collect lessons learned from AI acquisitions to enable sharing and application by other agencies.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an: The 2025 source, M-25-22, accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that deployed outcomes should outrank adoption counts and materially develops it into a lifecycle procurement framework. It requires agencies to connect performance incentives to mission outcomes and baseline performance, secure contractual rights for realistic testing and recurring evaluation, protect data and intellectual-property rights, reduce vendor lock-in, and reassess comparative effectiveness, risk and operating costs during deployment. It therefore contributes concrete acquisition mechanisms rather than merely endorsing outcome-focused governance. Material variation lies in the framework’s degree of prescription: some controls are mandatory, especially for high-impact uses, while others—such as periodic value reviews, interoperability measures and sunset criteria—are recommendations qualified by practicability. It also permits closely monitored vendor-run testing where appropriate and has phased applicability and national-security exclusions. Most importantly, the memorandum presents improved efficiency as an opportunity; it does not provide empirical evidence that AI deployments have already improved government services or that these safeguards will work universally.

elens.an: The curated sources assigned to the current wave accept the proposition that AI procurement should be judged by deployed outcomes and lifecycle value rather than adoption counts, demonstrations or initial price. They materially extend it in complementary ways. The Law of Evaluation develops a broader public-law architecture: causal comparison with existing practice, risk-tiered testing, continuing quality assurance, independent evaluation, funded expertise and enforceable access to testing materials. GAO grounds lifecycle governance in a nongeneralizable review of federal acquisitions, adding practical requirements around tailored contract terms, data rights, sustainment costs and systematic reuse of lessons from unsuccessful or limited-performing projects. Material variation lies mainly in method and confidence: the article advances prescriptive reforms for public and private buyers and argues that existing law can provide institutional scaffolding, while acknowledging risks of compliance theatre and political reversibility; GAO offers more bounded audit evidence, stresses testing and expertise constraints, and concludes that it is too early to identify a universally superior acquisition approach. These qualifications narrow the claims but do not challenge the proposition’s direction.

qs.q: Third, causal methods address the fundamental epistemic uncertainty about how AI systems will affect outcomes in the real world, moving beyond predictions about what might happen to evidence about what does happen once these systems are deployed.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

qs.q: OMB M-25-22 states that agencies should test proposed AI solutions to understand their capabilities and limitations before awarding contracts and should be able to regularly monitor and evaluate an AI system throughout its acquisition life cycle.[fn49] OMB M-25-22 also states that agencies should use data they have defined for validation and testing when conducting any independent evaluations.
